summary: This work demonstrates leakage elimination operator (LEO)-based adiabatic speedup on IBM superconducting quantum processors, achieving fidelities of $\sim 0.96$ at short evolution times ($T_{\mathrm{tot}} = \pi/2$) compared to $\sim 0.6$ without control. The results validate the feasibility of using ideal zero-area rectangular LEO pulses for accelerating adiabatic quantum computation while mitigating noise accumulation.
motivation: Adiabatic quantum computation faces an inherent trade-off: achieving adiabaticity requires slow evolution, but prolonged evolution times increase environmental noise damage, resulting in an optimal evolution time in realistic noisy systems. LEO control provides a theoretical strategy to realize adiabatic speedup over short timescales, but hardware implementation on superconducting processors was previously lacking.
method: Single-qubit adiabatic evolution from $|1\rangle$ to $(|0\rangle + |1\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ was implemented on the ibm\_marrakesh processor using Suzuki–Trotter digital simulation with ideal rectangular LEO pulses ($I = 40$, $\tau = \pi/20$) satisfying zero-area conditions. A comprehensive noise model including $T_1 = 180.86$ µs, $T_2 = 94.15$ µs, and depolarizing noise was calibrated to match hardware behavior, and Bayesian optimization of Fourier-parameterized pulses was attempted to further improve performance.
result: Ideal LEO pulses increased adiabatic fidelity from $\approx 0.6$ to $> 0.96$ at $T_{\mathrm{tot}} = \pi/2$, demonstrating effective adiabatic speedup; Bayesian-optimized pulses showed modest additional improvement ($\sim 1.83\%$) in simulations but comparable or slightly lower fidelity on hardware ($F \approx 0.92$ at $T_{\mathrm{tot}} = \pi$), indicating that real device noise and unmodeled error sources limit the benefit of waveform optimization beyond ideal pulses.
